SearchAliases: the chick pecks and the hen taps at the same instant
Senses.Explanation: The chick pecking and hen tapping simultaneously figures perfectly timed mutual response, while later teachers also warn against fixing on simultaneity. The phrase is attested 238 times across 77 source files representing 76 works. A later record defines the image graph by graph: the chick pecks, the mother taps, and neither precedes the other. In the Chan record it names a matched teacher-student exchange and is extended into an 'eye,' a 'function,' and a 'responsive mechanism.' Nanyuan's repeatedly quoted public interview distinguishes possessing the eye from possessing the function, then says that when adepts meet they do not peck and tap: doing so at the same instant misses it. Yuanwu applies the phrase to Fayan's answer 'you are Huichao' and to teachers who respond to circumstances. This use as a technical description of timing in public exchange is the corpus-specific bend of the hatching image.

Senses.Explanation: To spend the summer residence (坐夏) is to remain for the summer observance at a monastery. Micang Daokai's authored regulation supplies the clearest institutional contrast: earlier communities had only the summer period, whereas his community also established a winter period. Dahui Zonggao asks how many people spending the summer truly carry out what they say, and Shuzhong Wuyun's verse describes spending it without leaving the premises. Zhongfeng Mingben deliberately extends the expression: while the unresolved raised saying remains under investigation, it is still the time of the summer residence even beyond a fixed ninety days. In Xueguan's record an unnamed monk aligns the Buddha's summer stay with the present monastery's residence and release. Senses.Explanation: To take a position athwart a passage so that nothing can get through. Chan records extend that spatial action to speech, distinctions, directions, and decisive crossings: what is blocked may be everyone's tongue, the ten directions, the critical crossing, or the thousand branching differences. In the Recorded Sayings of Yuanwu Foguo, Yuanwu Keqin answers an unnamed monk with 'sit athwart and block off the tongues of everyone under heaven' (坐斷天下人舌頭), says that 'emerging and submerging are all blocked off' (頭出頭沒悉皆坐斷), and records an unnamed questioning monk's conclusion, 'then one blocks off the ten directions' (坐斷十方). In his Blue Cliff Record, Yuanwu says Xuefeng Yicun's utterance naturally blocks off everyone's tongues and later describes Xuefeng's language as 'blocking off past and present' (坐斷古今). The Record of the Ancestral Guidelines preserves Yuanwu's imperatives 'block off the critical crossing; do not let ordinary or holy pass' (坐斷要津，不通凡聖) and 'block off Vairocana's crown; do not receive Śākyamuni's text' (坐斷毗盧頂，不稟釋迦文). Miyun Yuanwu calls 'the move that meets one head-on' (當頭一著) one that blocks the critical crossing, while Tianyin Yuanxiu says that blocking the thousand branching differences lets one return home at once. The compound is repeatedly attested and remains a transitive, spatially forceful action in these uses; the reviewed evidence does not use it to mean merely sitting quietly.

Senses.Note: “Sit astride heaven and earth” is an emphatic image of a position that leaves no outside ground. Miyun gives it for the host in a host-and-guest sequence; Yinyuan for what spans ancient and present. Shiqi says that even sitting so decisively leaves something unfinished. Hongzhi compares it with other ways of meeting the world. Jifei gives the phrase when both person and setting are taken away, and Yuanjie says two earlier elders lacked its bearing. The image is tested, not a permanent title.

Senses.Note: “Sit beyond the reward and transformation Buddhas” is a strong image of not lodging in an attained form. Poshan connects it with ceasing to seek outside; Wanru immediately turns from it toward helping others. Yinyuan warns against sinking into the idea of a great enlightenment. Baiyu links it to the loss of holy and ordinary distinctions. Miaoyun speaks the phrase in grief for his teacher; Yushan follows it by raising a whisk. These turns keep the image active rather than an isolated slogan.

Senses.Explanation: The saying pictures a person occupying a crucial crossing so completely that neither the ordinary nor the sacred gets through. Yuanwu Keqin uses it in a pointer for what remains beyond merely exposing a turn or seeing a scene, and in a hall address joins it to cutting off doubt and slipping the life-and-death barrier. Dahui Zonggao quotes Luopu Yuanan making the last word the secure barrier that reaches this crossing. Miyun Yuanwu says that looking straight through occupies it, then raises his staff and asks how communication occurs there. The records make it a position from which the usual ordinary-versus-sacred division cannot command passage, not a literal checkpoint or a claim that ordinary and sacred are identical.

Senses.Explanation: The seated Chan procedure is a regulated bodily activity with an assigned place, posture, duration, and hall orientation. The Baizhang monastic code's titled Rules for Sitting Chan section directs a quiet place, a thick seat, full or half cross-legged sitting, the left palm resting on the right with the two thumbs touching, an upright body with the ears aligned to the shoulders and the nose to the navel, the tongue against the upper palate, and slightly open eyes, and it preserves Fayun Yuantong's rebuke of sitting with closed eyes as a black mountain ghost cave ("於閒靜處厚敷坐物…謂黑山鬼窟"). It continues: think neither good nor evil; the moment a thought arises, notice it, ever awake, neither dull nor scattered; this is the essential procedure of sitting Chan, a gate of ease, and those who fall ill from it miss its essentials ("一切善惡都莫思量。念起即覺…坐禪乃安樂法門"). The Baizhang monastic code redacted by Dongyang Dehui gives an observable hall convention: the assembly faces inward as in ordinary sitting Chan, then turns outward when the drum sounds ("如尋常坐禪向內坐。鼓鳴則轉身向外坐。"). Guting Shanjian says that sitting upright without lying down for ten or twenty years, even one or two lives, is what the ancients called sitting Chan. Nanyue Huairang's tile exchange, Linji Yixuan's refusal, Baozhi and Zhaoqing Shengdeng's critiques, and Zhanran Yuancheng's attack on half-asleep sitting still target this recognizable seated procedure. They disagree about what it accomplishes or how it is performed; they do not erase the bodily referent. The separate sense below is reserved for passages that explicitly redefine the compound apart from sitting posture.

AlternateTargets: sitting Chan apart from bodily sitting
Senses.Note: Three exact anchors from three independent sources establish the non-postural redefinition. This split is not noun versus verb or approval versus criticism: bodily sitting, breath regulation, and hall orientation are compatible predicates of the first sense, while explicit not-sitting-or-lying and lying-all-day are incompatible with that procedural referent. Huineng supplies the positive non-postural definition rather than an outside explanation.

Senses.Explanation: Non-postural sitting Chan is the compound explicitly redefined apart from the seated body. Huineng asks what is named sitting Chan and answers with two inward and relational predicates: toward good and bad circumstances outside, thoughts not arising is named sitting; inwardly seeing one's own nature unmoved is named Chan ("外於一切善惡境界，心念不起，名為坐；內見自性不動，名為禪"). Nanyue Huairang tells Mazu that if he is learning sitting Chan, Chan is not sitting or lying ("若學坐禪禪非坐臥"). Fu Dashi's verse makes the incompatibility visible by saying, “sitting Chan, lying down all day” ("坐禪終日臥"). These passages do more than praise, criticize, or reinterpret the seated procedure: they remove bodily sitting as the referent's necessary condition. That non-postural thing is therefore separated from the regulated cross-legged procedure above.

Senses.Explanation: To depart while seated or die while standing names a conspicuous death display used as evidence of command at life’s end; Chan masters repeatedly preserve the display while refusing to let it prove understanding by itself. Wansong Xingxiu, Guting Shanjian, Zhanran Yuancheng, Yingning Jing, and Wuyi Yuanlai all work the Jiufeng case: a head monk dies seated after staking his claim on understanding Shishuang, but Jiufeng says that seated departure or standing death does not reach the former master’s intent. Their later verdicts differ—Zhanran turns the criticism back on Jiufeng, while Wuyi faults both sides—but all distinguish the feat from the point being tested. Yulin Tongxiu uses the same paired phrase in a warning about death conduct: dying seated or standing when a lifespan is complete is separated from throwing away life before one’s conditions are exhausted. This confirms that the phrase denotes the observable manner of dying, not awakening or authority automatically. The entry describes a claimed demonstration at death. It neither denies that the feat occurs nor accepts it as sufficient proof of understanding; the corpus explicitly contests that inference.

Senses.Explanation: Sitting, lying down, and walking about is a compact enumeration of ordinary bodily postures that extends a statement across daily activity. Yun'e Xi places the postures beside seeing and hearing; Guting Shanjian places them beside dressing and eating while distinguishing masters, students, and common people; Baichi Yuanshuo says that through them he does not venture to open his mouth. Hanxiu Ruqian again pairs the list with dressing and eating and says Shakyamuni is met continually and Bodhidharma encountered everywhere. Poshan Haiming says the postures are “just this,” while Chushi Fanqi’s farewell verse says they expend no effort after eating on the long platform. Caoshan Baoji Xiong turns the list into a public challenge about whose share it is; Xisou Shaotan places it under a twelve-period warning to guard against the six thieves. The four graphs enumerate circumstances rather than an ordered exercise: the texts neither prescribe durations nor turn the postures into a manual.

Senses.Note: While picking tea, Yangshan shakes a tree after Guishan says he hears his voice but cannot see his form. Guishan replies, “You have grasped only its use, not its body.” Fushi sees the exchange as making trouble until the final threatened blows; Baichi questions whether either elder has shown body and use together. Liangting asks where the fault lies, while Lianfeng would rebuke both. The line is a judgment within a live exchange, not an abstract definition.

Senses.PreferredTarget: The chick pecks, the mother taps; the chick awakens and the mother breaks the shell
AlternateTargets: The chick and mother answer each other at the shell as awakening breaks through
SearchAliases: chick pecks mother taps shell awakening
Senses.Note: Xiangyan's longer verse continues by letting both mother and chick disappear and describing a response that meets conditions without error. Hanyue and Ruibai each put their own lines after the old verse. Liangting uses the opening pair in a memorial for his mother, moving its teacher-student image into a family relation. A questioner cites Xiangyan to Jiqi, who answers each part, while Hanxiu challenges a shallow account of simultaneous tapping. The pair carries both sides of the exchange; neither the mother nor the chick alone completes it.

Senses.Explanation: “The intricate knot and woven pattern” names a densely interlocked point that the Chan record treats as resistant to ordinary verbal handling. Mi’an Xianjie asks where it ultimately lies; Pinjixiang Zhixiang lifts a ruyi and asks what response there is to it, warning that ordinary people may not pass through; Dahui Zonggao says that at such a place it cannot be passed on or explained to another. These are questions and warnings around one fixed four-graph image, not separate senses or definitions of its individual graphs. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.

Senses.Explanation: Fenggan is the named Tiantai figure placed at Guoqing monastery whom later Chan masters bring into verses, travel imagery, public instruction, and rhetorical questions. Xuefeng Huikong's old-case verse sets Hanshan's handclap beside Fenggan's laugh. Gulin Qingmao's poem for a monk travelling to Tiantai names Fenggan and Shide as fitting companions. In both, Fenggan is a person inside a later master's authored verse, not its speaker. Dawei raises the report that old Fenggan meant to visit Wutai and asks who in his assembly could answer in Manjusri's place. An unnamed monk before Yi'an Shanzan asks why Fenggan must add more words. These public uses draw on Fenggan as a recognizable case figure while leaving each headword-bearing voice with the later speaker.
